entries.what_happened: Nine manuscripts in the family each take the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with zero initial velocity and a prescribed smooth external force f built by an effective algorithm from a Turing machine M and input w. Each shows that a fixed particle (or, in one case, a fixed velocity test) detects whether M halts, and each gives a unique classical solution in a stated class, which is smooth and global. Per manuscript: (1) Finite Instructions and Solenoidal Shear Flows: unit flat torus T^3, force divergence-free and mean-zero, periodic only after a one-unit loading interval; particle (1/8,3/8,1/2) enters {1/2<x<1} iff M halts; derivatives globally bounded, kinetic energy bounded. (2) A Fixed Particle Test for Computation in a Forced Viscous Flow: unit torus, mean-zero force (a divergence-free variant with the same velocity is also given); particle (1/8,3/8,0) enters {1/2<x<1} iff M halts; force and velocity derivatives bounded and in L^2 in time in sup norm. (3) Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary Navier-Stokes Forcing: unit torus, mean-zero force, time-independent for t>=1 via a ramp from rest; particle (1/4,1/4,0) enters {1/32<Y<1/8} iff M halts. Also a periodic-from-time-zero corollary, and a slow-clock variant with force and velocity derivatives O((1+t)^{-1-h}). (4) Geometric Programs for Solenoidal Forcing: unit torus, divergence-free mean-zero force periodic from time zero; particle (1/4,1/2,1/4) enters {1/2<x_1<7/8} iff M halts. Separately, a general sheet theorem realizes diagonal maps on T_10^3 with no halting event. (5) Prefix Instructions and Incompressible Flows: unit torus, mean-zero force (divergence not asserted zero), period one after t>=1 following a loader; particle (1/8,1/4,1/4) enters {1/2<x_1<1} iff M halts; alternative realizations use boxes, normal compensation, invariant planes. (6) Computation under Rapidly Vanishing Navier-Stokes Forcing: three memory constructions. Addressed: force on R^3 supported in a fixed compact box, all derivatives decaying faster than any power of (1+t); origin particle enters {X_1<-1} iff M halts. Alternating: fixed compact spatial support, same decay with (1+t+|X|); particle (-1,0,0) reaches {X_1>0} iff M halts. Lattice: unit torus, mean-zero force, derivatives decaying faster than any power; particle (1/4,1/2,1/2) enters {1/2<x_1<1 mod 1} iff M halts; a solenoidal variant has the same velocity. (7) Velocity-Field Detection of Computation in Forced Navier-Stokes Flows: no particle. On the unit torus, the event is that u_3 exceeds 1/2 somewhere on {1/32<y<1/8} at some time; the force is supported in K x T with K compact in (0,1)^2 and its derivatives are bounded only on finite time intervals. On R^2 x T, the event is that the integral of u_3 over {X_2>0} x T exceeds 1/2 at some time; the force has globally bounded mixed derivatives and compact horizontal support on each finite interval. (8) Scalar Potentials and Slow Clocks for Forced Fluid Computation: R^3 force with one compact spatial support for all time and derivatives O((1+t)^{-1-j}); origin particle enters {x_1<-1} iff M halts. Torus variant: particle (1/4,1/2,1/2) enters {1/2<x_1<1} with the same decay. Expanded-plane variant: observation u_3>1/2 on a fixed set, via the velocity-field theorem of entry (7). (9) Incompressible Box Transport and Finite Computation (October 6 version): a balanced three-stack recorder gives an R^3 force with one compact spatial support, bounded mixed derivatives, one-periodic after a one-unit loading interval, affine in viscosity (f = f_0 + nu f_1, with one velocity U); particle (4,0,0) enters (-1,2)^3 iff M halts. Further variants: torus charts, periodicity from time zero, bounded or slab observers, and slow clocks giving L^2-in-time forces.
entries.delivers: Nothing toward the Clay problem. The common result is a computability statement about forced flows: for a prescribed force, the zero-data equation has a unique smooth global solution in a stated class, and a particle event is equivalent to halting. Against the four alternatives: (A) and (B) ask about zero forcing and smooth data for all data on R^3 and T^3; every force in the family is nonzero and is defined as the residual of a chosen velocity, so none addresses zero-force global existence. (C) and (D) ask whether smooth data with smooth finite-energy forcing can lead to finite-time breakdown; no manuscript proves or constructs a singularity, and each asserts global smooth solutions for its own forces. The manuscripts disclaim regularity for arbitrary data: Finite Instructions says its existence result concerns 'this constructed family of forces, not regularity for arbitrary Navier-Stokes data', and Scalar Potentials says it makes 'no assertion about arbitrary-data regularity'. The matching pass's description ('a computability result about the equations though not a regularity or blow-up result') is accurate. The family does not claim to settle the problem, so no statement-match check arises.
entries.remains: All four alternatives remain open. The family says nothing about: whether smooth global solutions exist for all smooth finite-energy data with zero force on R^3 or T^3 (A, B); or whether some smooth data and smooth finite-energy forcing produce finite-time breakdown on R^3 or T^3 (C, D).
entries.direction: none toward the problem; constructs globally smooth forced solutions whose particle paths encode halting (no regularity or blow-up result)
entries.object: No counterexample or blow-up object. Each construction effectively builds an explicit smooth global solution (U, p) for its own forcing from (M, w). These are algorithmic constructions, not closed-form objects, and none is a counterexample to any Clay alternative.
entries.conditional_on: No unproven hypothesis bears on the Clay alternatives. Internal dependencies: the torus and R^2 x T velocity-field theorems of Velocity-Field Detection use the planar processor of Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary (its Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.1) and the uniqueness and projection lemmas of A Fixed Particle Test (Lemmas 3 and 1, cited as entry2026 and CompanionA). Scalar Potentials' expanded-plane corollary imports Velocity-Field Detection's Theorem 3.1. Box Transport's input-offset corollary imports Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary's planar processor and spatial clock. Rapidly Vanishing's realization, uniqueness and projection lemmas are cited from A Fixed Particle Test (Lemmas 3 and 1).
entries.doubts: Points from the text: (1) Finite Instructions does not quantify the radius of the positive neighborhood in its period-map statement, and it does not assert periodicity from time zero. (2) Velocity-Field Detection: torus derivative bounds may grow with the time interval, and its thresholds rest on heat-kernel constants of 10^9 or 10^8 and a total horizontal mass below 10^-11, proved in a lemma I did not read. (3) Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary: the autonomous clock argument asserts that each planar segment stays in the corridor J* where the spatial clock equals one. That assertion comes from the processor theorem, which I did not read. (4) Scalar Potentials: its stationary expanded-plane choice has nonzero mean force during startup, and its u_3 corollary asserts no large-time amplitude bound. (5) Rapidly Vanishing: observation is exact with no uniform margin; in the addressed construction the nonhalting first coordinate sits exactly on the boundary of the open detector, and the paper disclaims finite-precision robustness. (6) Geometric Programs' general sheet theorem is stated on T_10^3, not the unit torus.
